standard.title: Analyse civic perspectives and interpretations
standard.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have analysed information to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations at Year 9 (AC9HC9S03). They can examine media and information sources for varying views on contemporary issues.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations, including assessing the effectiveness of global governance institutions.

nodes.label: Identifying differences in perspectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different perspectives and interpretations in information about a political, legal or civic issue, explaining what positions different actors hold and why.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different perspectives on a political, legal or civic issue and explain why each actor holds their position.
nodes.typical_width: Examine information from traditional and social media sources to identify different views on and responses to a contemporary Australian political, legal or civic issue — including perspectives from government, advocacy groups, affected communities, and independent commentators.
wider: Examine how the same civic issue is framed differently across media platforms and analyse what the differences reveal about underlying values or interests

Identify perspectives from groups directly affected by a policy (e.g. communities subject to detention policies, First Nations Australians affected by land rights legislation) and compare with official government framing
Investigate how an international body (e.g. UN, ICC) interprets a situation differently from the Australian Government and evaluate what explains the difference
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can identify positions but cannot explain why different actors hold them are stuck at description — they cannot evaluate the quality or legitimacy of perspectives in the next node without understanding the interests, values and evidence behind each view.

response_modes.reason: Teach perspective analysis as requiring explanation of motive and interest, not just labelling (e.g. 'Group A supports X because...' not 'Group A supports X'). Model the move from identification to explanation.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two different perspectives on the issue
Explains why each actor holds their position (not just what it is)
Distinguishes between factual disagreements and value-based disagreements

nodes.label: Evaluating perspectives and interpretations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations, assessing the quality of evidence and reasoning behind each, including identifying value positions.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate at least two perspectives on an issue, identifying the values positions behind each and offering a supported judgement about which is better supported by evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations across sources — assessing the quality of evidence, internal consistency, and the values positions of different actors — and explain what the differences reveal about the civic issue.
wider: Examine the role of global governance institutions (e.g. UN, ICC) and evaluate their effectiveness in upholding democratic norms and human rights, comparing their interpretation with that of the Australian Government

Investigate a contemporary international event — armed conflict, international agreement, humanitarian disaster — and assess the values positions of different global actors (NGOs, governments, the Australian Government)
Evaluate how restrictions on freedoms (movement, trade, association) are justified differently by different actors and assess which justifications best align with democratic values

response_modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to distinguish between their own values and the standards of evidence they are applying. Scaffold this with explicit criteria: What makes an interpretation well-supported? What makes a values position coherent with democratic principles?

The global governance institution direction is a qualitatively different context — evaluating the UN or ICC involves multi-actor international settings where perspectives are structured differently than in domestic civic debate.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evaluating global governance institutions is substantively richer than evaluating domestic perspectives — it requires students to apply democratic norms to institutions operating in a context without the same enforcement mechanisms, raising deeper questions about legitimacy and effectiveness.
success_criteria: Evaluates at least two perspectives, identifying the values positions behind each
Assesses which perspective is better supported by evidence, with reasons
Explains what the differences in interpretation reveal about the underlying civic issue

nodes.label: Assessing effectiveness of global governance actors
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate a contemporary international event or situation and assess the effectiveness and values positions of global actors, including the Australian Government's response.
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate a contemporary international event or situation and identify the values positions of at least two global actors, including the Australian Government.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate a contemporary international event or situation — armed conflict, development of an international agreement, or natural or humanitarian disaster — to assess the effectiveness and values positions of global actors such as NGOs, and evaluate the Australian Government's response.
wider: Compare the responses of at least two different global actors (e.g. an NGO, a government, a multilateral body) to the same event and evaluate which response was most effective and why
Trace how the Australian Government's response to a specific international event has evolved over time and evaluate what drove the changes
Investigate a case where NGO action achieved outcomes that government actors could not and analyse what this reveals about the civic landscape of global governance

response_modes.reason: Integration node — analysis of global actors, evaluation of perspectives, and assessment of the Australian Government's role are brought together in a specific case study. Teaching investment is in supporting synthesis across the multiple actors and evidence sources.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two global actors and their values positions in relation to a specific international event
Assesses the effectiveness of at least one actor's response with evidence
Evaluates the Australian Government's response to the event
